extracted.intended_audience: electric cooperative leaders, co-op members, energy policymakers, and advocates preparing comments to EPA or following grid reliability policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reporting aimed at electric cooperatives and their members about the EPA proposed power-plant rule, its impacts on grid reliability and affordability, and related federal grant/permit processes — useful for preparing advocacy/notice-and-comment responses and policy engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on nascent technologies / technology readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal hinges on the widespread adoption of nascent technologies: clean hydrogen and carbon capture and storage. While both technologies are promising, they are not yet widespread or commercially available and have not been 'adequately demonstrated' as required by the Clean Air Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly notes these technologies are 'unproven', 'not ready for prime time', and 'will not be available within the compliance timeframe.' Comments should challenge regulatory reliance on technologies that lack commercial-scale demonstration and realistic availability within the rule's deadlines. Consider documenting technology readiness, commercial availability, and deployment timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority / major questions doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal violates the Clean Air Act by giving the EPA vast new authority of major economic and political significance without a clear statement from Congress. This disregards the 'major questions doctrine' and is inconsistent with the text, structure, and context of Clean Air Act Section 111.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocacy should argue whether the agency has statutory authority to impose the rule's requirements; explain statutory text/structure and apply major questions doctrine reasoning. Provide legal analysis or cite authority showing inconsistency with Section 111 where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic / achievable timelines and feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rules contain timelines that are unrealistic and unachievable. The compliance deadlines endanger new and existing natural gas plants and all but ensure coal units will opt to shut down by 2035.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should assess feasibility against infrastructure, permitting, supply chain, cost, public opposition, and land-access constraints. Use concrete examples (construction lead times, permitting durations, supply chain delays) to show timelines are unattainable and quantify the expected impacts on generation availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on reliability and affordability
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rules threaten reliability and affordability. The energy future outlined by EPA 'will result in more blackouts, higher costs, and greater uncertainty for Americans.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue and provide evidence about how the rule would affect grid reliability (risk of blackouts, loss of baseload/dispatchable generation) and consumer costs. Use NERC assessments, utility operational data, and cost modeling to substantiate claims about outages and rate impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require independent technical reliability assessment (NERC/FERC involvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymakers should look to NERC for guidance before they pass rules that will impact the reliability of the grid; FERC should use its authority to have NERC assess the impact of the EPA proposal and weigh in during the federal interagency review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend that rulemaking be informed by independent technical reliability assessments (e.g., NERC studies) during interagency review. Comments can request formal reliability studies, scenario modeling, and explanation of how the rule preserves system adequacy under peak and contingency conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve existing generation until adequate replacements/reserves exist
rubrics_metrics.description: We need to preserve the existing generation fleet, no matter the fuel source, until adequate replacements and reserves are in place. Avoid disorderly retirement and elimination of baseload generation that will leave a deficit of dispatchable generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for transitional policies or exemptions that maintain dispatchable capacity until new resources and transmission are reliably operational; provide timelines and resource adequacy analyses showing replacement needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting process reform and limiting litigation delays
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting process costs too much and takes too long; policymakers should streamline federal permitting and limit how long legal challenges to federal permitting decisions can drag on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples of stalled projects (e.g., nearly two-decade delay upgrading transmission) and recommend specific administrative or statutory permitting reforms, timelines, or coordination mechanisms to shorten approval times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission build-out and interconnection capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: To integrate renewables and meet demand, we must build a 'boatload' of transmission — cited as 200,000 miles of transmission in the coming decades — and make it easier to obtain permits to expand systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should address transmission planning, siting, and permitting barriers; quantify needed transmission capacity and recommend expedited processes, incentives, or reforms that facilitate large-scale transmission deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply chain resilience and equipment availability
rubrics_metrics.description: International supply chain delays continue to stall needed improvements at electric co-ops; delivery dates keep changing and impede projects (e.g., delays obtaining high-side breakers and substations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document how supply-chain constraints affect project schedules and compliance with regulatory timelines. Propose realistic contingency timelines, domestic sourcing policies, or phased compliance tied to equipment availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel availability and operational resiliency (natural gas vulnerabilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of natural gas for power plants has been threatened by extreme weather events, creating reliability risks; events like Winter Storm Uri show people can die without reliable power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight fuel-security risks in comments and recommend measures to ensure dispatchable fuel availability during extreme weather (fuel diversity, fuel storage, operational standards). Provide historical examples and data on fuel supply interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal grant program conditions (DOE GRIP requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: GRIP recipients must match a portion of the federal cost and ensure the projects create high-quality local jobs that benefit economically challenged communities and cause minimal environmental impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating grant-funded projects, document cost-match commitments, job-quality metrics, benefits to disadvantaged communities, and environmental-impact minimization. Use these criteria to argue for or against particular projects or funding allocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: FEMA hazard mitigation grant eligibility and timeline conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: FEMA awards hazard mitigation grants to communities repeatedly impacted by weather events; jurisdictions can include essential infrastructure owners (like co-ops) in their funding requests. In one example, work funded by the grant must be completed before June 2025.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments or applications should demonstrate repeated disaster impacts, include essential infrastructure owners as eligible applicants, and plan to meet grant timelines and mitigation goals. Document cost-sharing, scope (e.g., elevating substations, building looped transmission), and long-term resilience benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of microgrid control modeling and DER integration to enhance reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools like PowerModelsONM help distribution operators evaluate a grid’s resilience, plan for recovery using every asset available (distribution automation, microgrids, DERs), and restore power in worst-case scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage testing and deployment of validated software tools (including hardware-in-the-loop testing) to plan microgrids and DER integration. Provide evidence of benefits (outage reduction, restoration strategies) and recommend pilot programs, testing protocols, and integration with planning tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy tactic: volume and content of public comments matter to agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the things that the EPA looks at is the volume of comments they're getting. When you get into the tens of thousands of comments, it gets their attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For notice-and-comment campaigns, mobilize large numbers of substantive, specific comments (not just form letters) and document local impacts. Use grassroots platforms, targeted messaging, and channels (links, QR codes) to increase participation and visibility.
